questions.q: A school mural shows a Sierpinski Gasket painted up to Step 4, and every hole is painted gold. How many gold holes does the mural have?

Mohan cuts a Sierpinski Carpet out of a square card of side 27 cm and stops at Step 2. His cutter runs once round the edge of every hole.
(a) How many holes of each size are there, and what are their sides?
(b) Find the total length his cutter travels.
questions.a: (a) Step 1 makes 1 hole of side 9 cm (the centre of the 27 cm square). Step 2 makes one hole in each of the 8 remaining 9 cm squares, each of side 3 cm: 8 holes of side 3 cm. (b) 1 × 4 × 9 + 8 × 4 × 3 = 36 + 96 = 132 cm.
s: Part (a): 1 hole of side 9 cm and 8 holes of side 3 cm

questions.q:
Arjun claims: 'At every step of the Sierpinski Gasket, the number of holes is (number of remaining triangles − 1) ÷ 2.'
(a) Test his claim at Steps 1, 2, 3 and 4.
(b) Using R(n + 1) = 3R(n) and H(n + 1) = H(n) + R(n), explain why, if the claim holds at one step, it must hold at the next.
(c) Is Arjun right?
questions.a: (a) Step 1: (3 − 1)/2 = 1 hole; Step 2: (9 − 1)/2 = 4; Step 3: (27 − 1)/2 = 13; Step 4: (81 − 1)/2 = 40. These match 1, 4, 13, 40. (b) If H(n) = (R(n) − 1)/2, then H(n + 1) = (R(n) − 1)/2 + R(n) = (3R(n) − 1)/2 = (R(n + 1) − 1)/2. (c) Yes, the claim holds at every step (it also holds at Step 0: (1 − 1)/2 = 0).
s: Part (b): shows H(n + 1) = (R(n + 1) − 1)/2 from the two rules
Part (c): verdict Yes, true at every step

questions.q: True or False: Step 2 of the Sierpinski Carpet cuts 8 holes while Step 1 cuts only 1, so Step 2 removes more of the starting square's area than Step 1 does. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Step 1 removes 1 square of area 1/9 of the start = 9/81. Step 2 removes 8 squares, each 1/9 of a Step-1 square, that is 1/81 of the start, so 8/81 in all. 8/81 is less than 9/81: Step 2 removes less area even though it cuts more holes.
s: Compares 9/81 removed at Step 1 with 8/81 at Step 2

questions.q: Megha draws a Sierpinski Gasket up to Step 3, then zooms her camera onto the bottom-left triangle of side half the original (the corner piece made at Step 1). What does the zoomed picture show?
questions.a: A Step 2 gasket

questions.q:
A Sierpinski Gasket is drawn from an equilateral triangle of side 64 cm and taken to Step 3.
(a) Find the side of each smallest remaining triangle.
(b) How many of these smallest triangles have a side lying along the bottom edge of the big triangle? Explain why no gap appears along that edge.
questions.a: (a) The side halves at every step: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 cm. (b) Only middle (inverted) triangles are ever removed, and no removed triangle shares any length of the outer edge (at most a corner point touches it), so the bottom edge stays fully covered by smallest triangles: 64 ÷ 8 = 8 of them.
s: Part (b): 8 triangles, since no removed triangle shares any length of the outer edge

questions.q:
Compare and analyse how fast holes appear in the Sierpinski Carpet and the Sierpinski Gasket.
(a) Make a table of remaining pieces and holes for Steps 0 to 4 for both fractals.
(b) For each fractal, find the first step at which the number of holes is more than 500.
(c) In each fractal, how many new holes are made at a step compared with the pieces remaining at the step before? Use this to explain why the carpet's holes grow so much faster.
(d) At Step 4, how many times as many holes does the carpet have as the gasket? Give the answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.a: (a) Carpet: pieces 1, 8, 64, 512, 4096; holes 0, 1, 9, 73, 585. Gasket: pieces 1, 3, 9, 27, 81; holes 0, 1, 4, 13, 40. (b) Carpet: Step 4 (585). Gasket: holes continue 121, 364, 1093, so Step 7. (c) In both, every piece remaining at a step gets exactly one new hole at the next step. The carpet keeps 8 pieces from each piece and the gasket only 3, so the carpet has far more pieces, and so far more new holes, at every step. (d) 585 ÷ 40 = 14.6, about 15 times.
s: Part (a): correct table for both fractals
Part (c): one new hole per remaining piece; 8 versus 3 pieces kept

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Sierpinski Gasket.
Statement 1: At Step 2 it has 9 remaining triangles and 4 holes.
Statement 2: All the holes at Step 3 are the same size.
Statement 3: The holes at any step equal the holes at the step before plus the triangles that remained at the step before.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
(a) At Step 3 of the Sierpinski Carpet, how many holes lie inside one of the 8 squares that remained at Step 1? Explain using self-similarity.
(b) Check that your answer accounts for all 73 holes at Step 3.
(c) Hence write a rule giving H(n + 1) from H(n) alone, and use it to find H(4).
questions.a: (a) Each Step-1 square goes through two more steps, so it looks like a Step-2 carpet and holds H(2) = 9 holes. (b) 1 central hole + 8 × 9 = 73. (c) H(n + 1) = 1 + 8 H(n); H(4) = 1 + 8 × 73 = 585, which matches 73 + 512.
s: Part (a): 9 holes, because each Step-1 square becomes a Step-2 carpet

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After Step 1, the Sierpinski Gasket has more holes than the Sierpinski Carpet.
Reason (R): At each step the gasket keeps 3/4 of the area it had, while the carpet keeps 8/9 of the area it had.
questions.a: A is false but R is true
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q:
(a) Find how many more squares remain at Step 3 of the Sierpinski Carpet than at Step 2.
(b) Explain why the number of holes added at Step 3 is 64 and not your answer to (a).
questions.a: (a) R3 − R2 = 512 − 64 = 448. (b) At Step 3 each of the 64 squares left at Step 2 has its centre removed, so exactly one new hole is made per square: 64 new holes (H3 = 9 + 64 = 73). The 448 counts the extra small squares created, not holes.
s: Part (b): one new hole per Step-2 square, so 64 new holes

questions.q:
A quiz card says: 'A Sierpinski Carpet started from a square of side 100 cm reaches a step where every smallest square has side exactly 4 cm, and a Sierpinski Gasket started from an equilateral triangle of side 100 cm reaches a step where every smallest triangle has side exactly 10 cm.'
(a) Show that the carpet part is impossible.
(b) Show that the gasket part is impossible.
(c) For each fractal, find the first step at which the smallest piece is shorter than the size on the card.
questions.a: (a) At Step n the smallest square has side 100 ÷ 3^n cm. For this to be 4 cm we need 3^n = 25, but the powers of 3 go 1, 3, 9, 27, ... and skip 25. (b) At Step n the smallest triangle has side 100 ÷ 2^n cm. For 10 cm we need 2^n = 10, but the powers of 2 go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... and skip 10. (c) Carpet: 100/9 ≈ 11.1 cm at Step 2 and 100/27 ≈ 3.7 cm at Step 3, so Step 3. Gasket: 12.5 cm at Step 3 and 6.25 cm at Step 4, so Step 4.
s: Part (a): needs 3^n = 25, which is not a power of 3
Part (b): needs 2^n = 10, which is not a power of 2
Part (c): carpet Step 3 (about 3.7 cm), gasket Step 4 (6.25 cm)

questions.q:
An art club will paint a Sierpinski Gasket on a wall, on a triangle of area 256 sq dm. Only the remaining triangles are painted; the holes stay bare. One tin of paint covers 120 sq dm and costs Rs 300. Each remaining triangle is masked with its own stencil, costing Rs 2 per triangle. The club wants at least Step 2 and will choose Step 2, 3 or 4.
(a) Find the area to be painted at Steps 2, 3 and 4.
(b) How many tins are needed at each of these steps?
(c) Find the stencil cost at each of these steps.
(d) Which step should the club choose to spend the least? Justify with the total cost of each step.
questions.a: (a) Each step keeps 3/4 of the area: Step 2: 256 × 9/16 = 144 sq dm; Step 3: 108 sq dm; Step 4: 81 sq dm. (b) Step 2 needs 2 tins (144 is more than 120); Steps 3 and 4 need 1 tin each. (c) Remaining triangles are 9, 27 and 81, so Rs 18, Rs 54 and Rs 162. (d) Totals: Step 2: 600 + 18 = Rs 618; Step 3: 300 + 54 = Rs 354; Step 4: 300 + 162 = Rs 462. Step 3 is cheapest: going to Step 4 saves no paint tin but costs more in stencils, and Step 2 needs a second tin.
s: Part (d): Step 3, totals Rs 618, Rs 354 and Rs 462

questions.q:
Match each description with its value.
Column A:
1. Remaining squares of a carpet at the step where the smallest square's side is 1/27 of the starting side
2. Holes in a carpet at the step where 64 squares remain
3. Remaining triangles of a gasket started from side 48 cm, at the step where the smallest side is 3 cm
4. Holes in a gasket at the step where 27 triangles remain
Column B:
(P) 81
(Q) 9
(R) 13
(S) 512

A designer changes the carpet rule: at each step every square is divided into 9 and the centre AND the four corner squares are removed, keeping only the 4 edge-middle squares. Starting from one square, how many smallest squares remain at Step 3?
A carpet weaver in Bhadohi starts with a square of cloth of side 81 cm and follows the Sierpinski Carpet rule up to Step 3. How many smallest squares remain at Step 3, and what is the side of each?
questions.a: 512 squares of side 3 cm

questions.q:
A Sierpinski Carpet is to be drawn on squared paper so that every corner of every remaining square at Step 3 falls exactly on a grid point.
(a) What is the smallest possible side of the starting square, in grid units?
(b) For that square, how many unit grid squares are still part of the carpet at Step 3?
questions.a: (a) Each step divides the side by 3, so after 3 steps the smallest square has side (side)/27. For that to be a whole number of units, the side must be a multiple of 27; the smallest is 27 units. (b) The smallest squares are then 1 unit each, and 8^3 = 512 of them remain.
s: Part (a): 27 units, since the side is divided by 3 three times

questions.q:
A Sierpinski Gasket starts from an equilateral triangle of side 32 cm.
(a) Find the side of the smallest remaining triangles at Steps 1, 2 and 3.
(b) Find the number of remaining triangles and of holes at Step 3.
(c) At Step 3 the holes are of three sizes. Give the side of each size and how many holes there are of each, and check the total against (b).
(d) Taking the area of the starting triangle as 1 sq unit, find the area remaining at Step 3.
(e) At which step does the remaining area first fall below one-half of the start?
questions.a: (a) 16 cm, 8 cm, 4 cm (the side halves each step). (b) 3^3 = 27 triangles; holes 1 + 3 + 9 = 13. (c) The Step-1 hole has side 16 cm (1 hole), the Step-2 holes side 8 cm (3 holes), the Step-3 holes side 4 cm (9 holes): 1 + 3 + 9 = 13. (d) Each step keeps 3/4, so (3/4)^3 = 27/64 sq unit. (e) Step 1: 3/4; Step 2: 9/16 (more than 1/2); Step 3: 27/64 (less than 32/64). So Step 3.
s: Part (c): 1 hole of side 16, 3 of side 8, 9 of side 4

questions.q:
A Jaipur design school wants a fractal cut-out panel for its gate. The panel must have at least 50 holes, and the laser cannot cut a hole whose side is less than 3 cm. The laser shop charges Rs 2 per hole, whatever its size, and the budget is Rs 200.
Design P: a Sierpinski Carpet from a square of side 81 cm.
Design Q: a Sierpinski Gasket from an equilateral triangle of side 96 cm.
(a) For Design P, find the first step with at least 50 holes and the side of its smallest hole.
(b) For Design Q, find the first step with at least 50 holes and the side of its smallest hole.
(c) Find the laser cost of each design at the step found.
(d) Which design should the school choose? Justify using all three conditions.
questions.a: (a) Carpet holes: 1, 9, 73, so Step 3. The smallest hole is the centre of a Step-2 square of side 9 cm, so its side is 3 cm. (b) Gasket holes: 1, 4, 13, 40, 121, so Step 5. The smallest hole is the middle of a Step-4 triangle of side 96/16 = 6 cm, so its side is 3 cm. (c) P: 73 × 2 = Rs 146. Q: 121 × 2 = Rs 242. (d) Design P. Both meet the 50-hole and 3 cm conditions, but Q costs Rs 242, over the Rs 200 budget, while P costs Rs 146.
s: Part (d): chooses P, as only P fits the budget while both meet the other two conditions

questions.q: A Sierpinski Carpet is cut from a square of side 81 cm and taken to Step 4. The number of its holes whose side is exactly 3 cm is ___. (Write the number in digits.)
A wall hanging is cut from a 90 cm × 90 cm square of felt following the Sierpinski Carpet rule up to Step 2. How much felt is left in the hanging?
questions.a: 6400 sq cm

questions.q:
A Koch Snowflake is drawn from an equilateral triangle of side 54 cm.
(a) How many triangles are raised at Step 2, and what is the side of each?
(b) Tanvi says: 'The bumps added at Step 2 add the same length to the boundary as the bumps added at Step 1.' Check her claim.
questions.a: (a) Step 1 leaves 12 sides of 18 cm. At Step 2 one triangle is raised on the middle third of each, so 12 triangles of side 6 cm. (b) Each bump removes one middle part and adds two sides of the same length, so it adds one side-length to the boundary. Step 1: 3 bumps of 18 cm add 54 cm (162 cm to 216 cm). Step 2: 12 bumps of 6 cm add 72 cm (216 cm to 288 cm). She is wrong: Step 2 adds more.
s: Part (b): 54 cm added at Step 1 against 72 cm at Step 2, so the claim is wrong

questions.q: A student builds a model tower in the spirit of the Kandariya Mahadev Temple. The main tower is 32 cm tall and carries 3 smaller copies of itself, each half as tall as the structure it sits on. Each copy carries 3 still smaller copies in the same way, and so on, for 4 levels of copies below the main tower. How many copies are at the smallest level, and how tall is each?
questions.a: 81 copies, each 2 cm tall

questions.q:
A jeweller bends silver wire into Koch Snowflake pendants. Each pendant must use one piece of wire, at most 150 cm long, and she cannot bend a side shorter than 0.5 cm.
(a) For a starting triangle of side 9 cm, find the perimeter at Steps 0, 1, 2 and 3.
(b) For side 9 cm, what is the highest step she can bend?
(c) For side 9 cm, which limit stops her first, the wire or the bending? Show the step each limit allows.
(d) For a starting side of 18 cm, find the highest step that meets both limits.
(e) She can choose a starting side of 9 cm or 18 cm. Which gives the more detailed pendant, and how much more wire does it need? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3: 27, 36, 48 and 64 cm. (b) The side goes 9, 3, 1, 1/3 cm: Step 2 (1 cm); at Step 3 the side, 1/3 cm, is too short. (c) Bending. The wire allows up to Step 5 (perimeter about 113.8 cm; Step 6 needs about 151.7 cm), but bending stops her at Step 2. (d) Sides 18, 6, 2, 2/3 cm and perimeters 54, 72, 96, 128 cm. Step 3 has side 2/3 cm (at least 0.5 cm) and needs 128 cm (within 150 cm). Step 4 fails both: side 2/9 cm and about 170.7 cm of wire. So Step 3. (e) The 18 cm start: it reaches Step 3 against Step 2 for 9 cm, because a larger start keeps the sides long enough for one more step. It takes 128 − 48 = 80 cm more wire, which is within the limit.
s: Part (b): Step 2, since Step 3 sides are 1/3 cm
Part (c): bending stops her at Step 2, the wire would last to Step 5
Part (d): Step 3 (side 2/3 cm, 128 cm of wire)
Part (e): 18 cm, one more step for 80 cm more wire

questions.q: A Diwali lantern frame is shaped like a Koch Snowflake made up to Step 2 from an equilateral triangle of side 27 cm. How long a ribbon is needed to go once around its edge?
questions.a: 144 cm

questions.q: Four students each write a rule for a pattern. Whose rule gives a self-similar pattern, the same design repeated at smaller and smaller scales?
questions.a: Split each square into 4, remove one corner square, repeat on each square left
o: Split each square into 4, remove one corner square, repeat on each square left
Split one square into 9 equal squares once, and then colour only its centre square
Place squares of side 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm in a row, each touching the next
Draw one large square, and then colour a small square at each of its four corners

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Koch Snowflake.
Statement 1: The number of sides is multiplied by 4 at each step.
Statement 2: The length of each side is divided by 4 at each step.
Statement 3: The perimeter at Step 2 is 8/3 times the perimeter of the starting triangle.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only

questions.q:
'A temple can only be fractal-like, while the Koch Snowflake is a true mathematical fractal.' Justify this statement using the model below.
As a model, a temple tower 27 m tall carries 4 smaller copies of itself, each one-third as tall as the structure it sits on; each copy carries 4 still smaller copies in the same way, and so on. A carver cannot carve a copy shorter than 10 cm.
(a) Find the heights of the copies at the first three levels.
(b) How many levels of copies can be carved?
(c) How many copies are there at the smallest level?
(d) A Koch Snowflake is drawn from a triangle of side 27 cm with a pen that cannot draw a side shorter than 1 mm. What is the last step that can be drawn?
(e) Use (b) and (d) to justify the statement.
questions.a: (a) 9 m, 3 m and 1 m. (b) Next come 1/3 m (about 33 cm), 1/9 m (about 11 cm) and 1/27 m (about 3.7 cm). Copies down to 11 cm can be carved, so 5 levels. (c) 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 1024 copies. (d) In millimetres the side goes 270, 90, 30, 10, 3.3, 1.1, 0.37: Step 5 (about 1.1 mm) can be drawn, Step 6 cannot. (e) Both real objects stop after a few repeats (5 levels, Step 5) because of a smallest size that can be made. The temple shows the same structure at smaller scales only for those levels, so it is fractal-like. The Koch Snowflake is defined by a rule that can be applied again at every scale, so the mathematical shape keeps repeating where a drawing or a carving must stop.
s: Part (b): 5 levels (11 cm allowed, 3.7 cm not)
Part (d): Step 5 (1.1 mm), not Step 6 (0.37 mm)
Part (e): real objects stop at a smallest size; the mathematical rule repeats at every scale

questions.q:
A science museum shows three Koch Snowflake panels, each labelled only with its number of sides. Panel X has 48 sides, Panel Y has 768 sides and Panel Z has 192 sides. On every panel the smallest side is 2 cm.
(a) At which step is each panel?
(b) Working backwards, find the side of the starting triangle for each panel.
(c) Find the perimeter of each panel.
(d) A visitor says: 'Panel Y's starting triangle had 4 times the side of Panel Z's, because Y has 4 times as many sides.' Judge his statement using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) 48 = 3 × 4^2, so X is Step 2; 768 = 3 × 4^4, so Y is Step 4; 192 = 3 × 4^3, so Z is Step 3. (b) The side is divided by 3 each step: X: 2 × 9 = 18 cm; Y: 2 × 81 = 162 cm; Z: 2 × 27 = 54 cm. (c) X: 48 × 2 = 96 cm; Y: 768 × 2 = 1536 cm; Z: 192 × 2 = 384 cm. (d) He is wrong about the triangle: 162 ÷ 54 = 3 times, not 4. It is the perimeter that is 4 times (1536 ÷ 384 = 4), because the sides are 4 times as many and all are 2 cm.
s: Part (a): X Step 2, Y Step 4, Z Step 3
Part (d): starting side is 3 times, perimeter is 4 times; statement wrong

questions.q: True or False: Two Koch Snowflakes at the same step always have the same number of sides, even when one starts from a much larger triangle than the other. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The number of sides starts at 3 and is multiplied by 4 at every step, so at Step n it is 3 × 4^n whatever the size of the triangle. The size only changes the length of each side and so the perimeter: at Step 2, snowflakes from triangles of side 9 cm and 27 cm both have 48 sides, but perimeters of 48 cm and 144 cm.
s: Sides depend only on the step (3 × 4^n); size changes only side length and perimeter

questions.q:
A weaver makes a blanket inspired by Fulani designs. The largest diamond has side 48 cm; inside it is a diamond with side half as long, inside that one another with side half as long again, and so on. She stops before any diamond would have a side shorter than 5 cm.
(a) How many diamonds are in the nest?
(b) She outlines every diamond with gold thread. How much thread does she need for the whole nest?
questions.a: (a) Sides 48, 24, 12, 6; the next would be 3 cm, shorter than 5 cm, so 4 diamonds. (b) Each diamond has 4 equal sides: 4 × (48 + 24 + 12 + 6) = 4 × 90 = 360 cm of thread.

questions.q:
A puzzle card claims: 'Some step of a Koch Snowflake has exactly 300 sides, and at some step its perimeter is exactly double the perimeter of the starting triangle.'
(a) Show that no step has 300 sides.
(b) Show that the perimeter is never exactly double.
(c) Between which two steps does the perimeter pass double the start?
questions.a: (a) The sides are 3 × 4^n: 3, 12, 48, 192, 768, ... 300 = 3 × 100 and 100 is not a power of 4 (it lies between 64 and 256), so no step has 300 sides. (b) Each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3, so at Step n it is 4^n/3^n times the start. Double would need 4^n = 2 × 3^n. For n = 0 this says 1 = 2; for n ≥ 1 the right side is a multiple of 3 but a power of 4 never is. So it is never exactly double. (c) Step 2 gives 16/9 (less than 2) and Step 3 gives 64/27 (more than 2), so it passes double between Steps 2 and 3.
s: Part (a): sides are 3 × 4^n, and 100 is not a power of 4
Part (b): 4^n = 2 × 3^n is impossible (multiple of 3 on one side only)

questions.q: Neel says: 'At each step of the Koch Snowflake, the number of sides is multiplied by 4, so the perimeter is multiplied by 4 too.' Test both halves of his statement for a snowflake that starts from a triangle of side 9 cm, going from Step 0 to Step 1, and give your verdict.
questions.a: Sides: 3 at Step 0 and 12 at Step 1, so the number of sides is multiplied by 4 (first half right). Perimeter: 27 cm at Step 0; at Step 1 each side is 3 cm, so 12 × 3 = 36 cm. 36 ÷ 27 = 4/3, not 4 (second half wrong), because each new side is one-third as long. Verdict: partly right.
s: Perimeter: 27 cm to 36 cm, multiplied by 4/3 because each side is one-third as long
Verdict: partly right (sides yes, perimeter no)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Going from Step 1 to Step 2, a Koch Snowflake gains 36 sides.
Reason (R): At every step, each side of the shape is replaced by 4 sides.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: The perimeter of a Koch Snowflake at Step 3 is 128 cm. Its perimeter at Step 1 was ___ cm. (Write the number in digits.)

Both the Koch Snowflake and the Sierpinski Gasket start from an equilateral triangle.
(a) State the difference in what each step does to the triangle.
(b) Give one consequence of this difference for the outer boundary of the shape at Step 2.
questions.a: (a) The Koch step adds: it raises new triangles outward on every side. The gasket step removes: it cuts the middle triangle out from inside each remaining triangle. (b) The snowflake's outline gets longer (Step 2 perimeter is 16/9 of the start), while the gasket's outer boundary stays the original triangle, with the same perimeter; only holes appear inside.
s: Part (a): Koch adds outward bumps; the gasket removes inner triangles
Part (b): Koch outline grows (16/9 of the start), gasket outline unchanged

questions.q: In a model of a lizard-ring design inspired by Escher's 'Smaller and Smaller', there are rings of identical lizards. The outer ring has 6 lizards, each 32 cm long. Each ring further in has lizards half as long as the ring outside it, and twice as many of them. How many lizards are in the ring whose lizards are 4 cm long?
questions.a: 48 lizards

questions.q:
A Koch Snowflake is made from an equilateral triangle and taken to Step 3.
(a) How many new small triangles are raised outward at Step 3?
(b) How many triangles have been raised in all, from Step 1 to Step 3?
questions.a: (a) One triangle is raised on every side of the Step-2 shape, which has 3 × 4^2 = 48 sides, so 48. (b) 3 (Step 1) + 12 (Step 2) + 48 (Step 3) = 63.
s: Part (a): 48, one per side of the Step-2 shape

questions.q: A printer traces Koch Snowflake steps starting from an equilateral triangle of side 81 mm, but it cannot print a side shorter than 2 mm. What is the highest step it can print, and how many sides does that step have?
questions.a: Step 3, with 192 sides

questions.q:
(a) At which step does a Koch Snowflake first have more than 1000 sides?
(b) If every side at that step is exactly 1 cm, what was the side of the starting triangle?
questions.a: (a) Sides: 3, 12, 48, 192, 768, 3072. Step 5 is the first above 1000. (b) The side is divided by 3 five times, so the start was 3^5 = 243 cm.

questions.q:
A Hyderabad school team draws a Koch Snowflake outline in coloured powder for a rangoli contest. They start from an equilateral triangle of side 81 cm. Their bag of powder can draw a line at most 600 cm long, and the judges award points for detail, so the team wants the highest step the powder allows.
(a) Find the number of sides and the length of each side at Step 2.
(b) Find the perimeter at Step 2 and at Step 3.
(c) A teammate predicts the Step 4 perimeter by adding to the Step 3 perimeter the same increase as from Step 2 to Step 3. Find her prediction and the correct value.
(d) Which step should the team draw? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 3 × 4^2 = 48 sides, each 81 ÷ 9 = 9 cm. (b) Step 2: 48 × 9 = 432 cm. Step 3: 192 × 3 = 576 cm. (c) Her prediction: 576 + 144 = 720 cm. Correct: the perimeter is multiplied by 4/3 each step, 576 × 4/3 = 768 cm (768 sides of 1 cm). (d) Step 3: it needs 576 cm, within 600 cm, while Step 4 needs 768 cm, which the powder cannot cover.
s: Part (c): prediction 720 cm, correct 768 cm (growth is ×4/3, not a fixed amount)

questions.q:
A calculation reads: 27 × (4/3) × (4/3) × (4/3) = 64.
(a) Explain what 27, each factor 4/3, and the number of factors stand for if this is a Koch Snowflake perimeter.
(b) Find the side of the starting triangle.
(c) Write a short real-life situation that this calculation could describe.
questions.a: (a) 27 is the perimeter of the starting triangle; each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3; three factors means Step 3. (b) 27 ÷ 3 = 9 units. (c) For example: a rangoli border is drawn as a Koch Snowflake to Step 3 from a triangle of side 9 cm; the coloured line around it is 64 cm long.
s: Part (a): 27 is the starting perimeter, 4/3 the growth per step, three steps
Part (c): a sensible situation matching side 9 and Step 3

questions.q: For a Science Week display, Nisha builds a regular tetrahedron frame from 6 equal straws. She wants any two straws that do not touch each other at all to be the same colour, and straws that meet at a corner to be different colours. How many colours does she need?

Tara claims: 'Every net of a cube made of 1 cm squares has a perimeter of exactly 14 cm.'
(a) Check her claim for the cross-shaped net (a row of four squares with one square above and one below the second square).
(b) Six separate squares have 24 sides of 1 cm. A net of a cube always has exactly 5 joins between its squares. Use this to explain whether her claim holds for every net.
(c) State your verdict.
questions.a: (a) Counting the outline of the cross: 14 sides of 1 cm, so 14 cm. (b) Each join hides 2 sides (one from each square) from the outline, so the perimeter is 24 − 2 × 5 = 14 cm for every net. (c) Yes, Tara is right.

questions.q: A dice maker's net is a staircase of six squares: squares 1 and 2 side by side in the top row; square 3 directly below square 2, with square 4 to the right of square 3; square 5 directly below square 4, with square 6 to the right of square 5. When the net is folded into a cube, which number is on the face opposite 1?

A dodecahedron has 12 faces, each a pentagon, and exactly 3 faces meet at each of its corners.
(a) How many edges does it have? Explain.
(b) How many vertices does it have? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The 12 pentagons have 12 × 5 = 60 sides in all. Each edge of the solid is a side of exactly 2 faces, so there are 60 ÷ 2 = 30 edges. (b) The 12 pentagons have 60 corners in all, and each vertex of the solid is a corner of exactly 3 faces, so there are 60 ÷ 3 = 20 vertices.
s: Part (a): 60 ÷ 2 = 30 edges, each edge shared by 2 faces
Part (b): 60 ÷ 3 = 20 vertices, 3 faces at each corner

questions.q:
Compare and analyse two nets made by a student.
Net X (square pyramid): a square of side 6 cm with an isosceles triangle of sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm joined to each side of the square.
Net Y (triangular prism): three rectangles, each 4 cm wide and 10 cm tall, joined side by side along their 10 cm sides, with an equilateral triangle of side 4 cm joined to the top and to the bottom of the middle rectangle.
(a) How many faces and edges does each folded solid have, and how many folds does each net have?
(b) Find the number of segments on the outline of each net and the perimeter of Net X.
(c) Find the perimeter of Net Y.
(d) Explain why, for any net, the outline has 2 × (edges − folds) segments.
(e) Use the rule in (d) to predict the number of outline segments of any net of a hexagonal pyramid.
questions.a: (a) Square pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges. Triangular prism: 5 faces, 9 edges. A net is one piece, and each fold joins one more face, so each net has 5 − 1 = 4 folds. (b) Net X: the 4 square sides are folds, so the outline is the 8 slanting sides; perimeter 8 × 5 = 40 cm. Net Y has 10 outline segments. (c) Two 10 cm sides (left and right) and eight 4 cm sides (two rectangle tops, two rectangle bottoms and two sides of each triangle): 20 + 32 = 52 cm. (d) Each edge that is not a fold is cut open, and both of its sides lie on the outline; a fold does not appear on the outline. So the outline has 2 × (edges − folds) segments: 2 × (8 − 4) = 8 and 2 × (9 − 4) = 10, which agree with (b). (e) A hexagonal pyramid has 7 faces, so 6 folds, and 12 edges: 2 × (12 − 6) = 12 segments.
s: Part (a): 5 faces each, 8 and 9 edges, 4 folds each
Part (b): 8 and 10 segments; Net X perimeter 40 cm
Part (d): each cut edge appears twice on the outline, folds not at all

questions.q:
A toy house is a cube with a square pyramid fixed on top, the pyramid's square base covering the cube's top face exactly.
(a) Find the numbers of faces, edges and vertices of the toy house.
(b) Rohit adds the counts of a cube (6, 12, 8) and a square pyramid (5, 8, 5). Find his totals and explain why each one is too large.
questions.a: (a) Faces: 5 square faces of the cube + 4 triangles = 9. Edges: 12 of the cube + 4 slanting edges = 16. Vertices: 8 of the cube + the apex = 9. (b) His totals are 11, 20 and 13. The shared square is counted twice as a face but is inside the house, so it is not a face at all (2 too many). The 4 edges and 4 corners of that square are counted once for each solid, so edges and vertices are each 4 too many.
s: Part (b): totals 11, 20, 13; the shared square is not a face and its 4 edges and 4 vertices are counted twice

questions.q:
Each net in Column A is folded into a closed solid. Match each net with the numbers of edges and vertices of the solid it makes.
Column A:
1. Six equal squares
2. Two equilateral triangles and three equal rectangles
3. One square and four equal triangles
4. One regular hexagon and six equal triangles
Column B:
(P) 12 edges, 8 vertices
(Q) 9 edges, 6 vertices
(R) 8 edges, 5 vertices
(S) 12 edges, 7 vertices

A regular tetrahedron has edges of 6 cm.
(a) One of its nets is a single large equilateral triangle. Find the side of this triangle, and say how the four faces sit inside it.
(b) Its other net is a strip of four triangles: two point up, with their bases end to end along a bottom line from 0 cm to 12 cm; two point down, with their bases end to end along a top line from 3 cm to 15 cm across. Find the perimeter of each net.
questions.a: (a) The large triangle has side 12 cm: one face sits in the middle (upside down) and the other three are at the corners, each joined to one side of the middle face. (b) Large triangle: 3 × 12 = 36 cm. Strip: two long sides of 12 cm and two slanting ends of 6 cm, 12 + 12 + 6 + 6 = 36 cm. Both are 36 cm.
s: Part (a): side 12 cm, middle face with three corner faces

questions.q: Kabir cuts out equal equilateral triangles joined edge to edge in four different ways. Which cut-out can be folded into a closed regular tetrahedron?
questions.a: One triangle with another triangle joined to each of its sides

Five triangles in one long strip, pointing up and down in turn along it

questions.q: True or False: Any arrangement of 6 equal squares joined edge to edge, in which no row has more than 4 squares, can be folded into a cube. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Two rows of three squares, one row directly on the other (a 2 by 3 block), has no row longer than 3, but it cannot fold into a cube: four of its squares form a 2 by 2 block, which lies flat around one corner and cannot wrap round a cube corner, where only three faces meet. The squares overlap.
s: Gives a valid counter-example such as the 2 by 3 block, with the reason it overlaps

questions.q: A solid has two congruent triangles as opposite faces, joined by three rectangular faces. Riya calls it a triangular pyramid. What is the correct description?
questions.a: A triangular prism with 9 edges and 6 vertices

questions.q:
A board-game company prints dice from a net. The net has a row of four squares A, B, C, D from left to right, a square E attached above B, and a square F attached below C. On a proper die, the numbers on opposite faces add up to 7. A designer writes 1, 2, 3, 4 on A, B, C, D and 5, 6 on E, F.
(a) Which pairs of squares become opposite faces when the net is folded?
(b) Which of the designer's opposite pairs fail the 'add up to 7' rule?
(c) Give one way to renumber the squares so that the die is proper.
(d) A second designer moves F so that it is below D instead of C. Does this change which squares are opposite? Explain.
questions.a: (a) A and C, B and D, E and F (in a row of four that wraps round, squares two apart are opposite; the two squares off the row close the ends). (b) All three fail: 1 + 3 = 4, 2 + 4 = 6, 5 + 6 = 11. (c) For example A = 1, C = 6, B = 2, D = 5, E = 3, F = 4. (d) No. The row of four still wraps round the cube, so A–C and B–D stay opposite, and E and F still close the two open ends, so they are still opposite each other.
s: Part (c): a valid renumbering with each opposite pair adding to 7
Part (d): no change, with the wrapping-row reason

questions.q: On a cube-shaped wire frame, Ravi picks one edge. The number of the other edges that neither touch his edge nor run parallel to it is ___. (Write the number in digits.)
A packaging student cuts out four shapes, each of 6 equal squares joined edge to edge. Which one folds into a closed cube?
questions.a: A row of four squares, with one square above the second and one below the fourth
o: A row of four squares, with one square above the second and one below the fourth
A row of four squares, with one square above the first and one above the second
A row of five squares, with one more square above the middle square of the row
Two rows of three squares each, with one row placed directly on top of the other row

questions.q:
Akash claims: 'If I double the number of sides of a pyramid's base, the pyramid's faces double and its vertices double too.'
(a) Test his claim by going from a square pyramid to an octagonal pyramid.
(b) Write the faces of an n-sided pyramid and of a 2n-sided pyramid, and compare.
(c) Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) Square pyramid: 5 faces, 5 vertices. Octagonal pyramid: 9 faces, 9 vertices, not 10. (b) n + 1 becomes 2n + 1, while double would be 2n + 2: always 1 short. The same holds for vertices. (c) No, the claim is wrong; the counts never exactly double (only the edges, 2n to 4n, double).

questions.q:
A sweet shop orders boxes that are cuboids 12 cm long, 8 cm wide and 4 cm high, cut from card sheets 22 cm × 26 cm. Both possible layouts start with a column of four faces, each 12 cm wide: top (12 × 8), front (12 × 4), bottom (12 × 8), back (12 × 4), one under the other.
Layout A: the two end faces are attached to the left and right sides of the top face.
Layout B: the two end faces are attached to the left and right sides of the front face.
(a) What are the measurements of each end face?
(b) Find the length and width of the smallest rectangle that holds Layout A.
(c) Find the same for Layout B.
(d) Which layout should the shop use for these sheets? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Each end face is 8 cm × 4 cm. (b) The column is 12 cm wide and 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 24 cm tall. In Layout A each end face meets the top face along its 8 cm side, so it sticks out 4 cm on each side: 4 + 12 + 4 = 20 cm by 24 cm. (c) In Layout B each end face meets the front face along its 4 cm side, so it sticks out 8 cm: 8 + 12 + 8 = 28 cm by 24 cm. (d) Layout A: 20 cm × 24 cm fits on a 22 cm × 26 cm sheet; Layout B needs 28 cm, more than either side of the sheet.
s: Part (d): Layout A, since only it fits 22 × 26

questions.q:
A gift box is a cuboid 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 3 cm high.
(a) List the sizes of the six rectangles in its net.
(b) In one net, four of the faces form a single strip that wraps once around the box, every face in the strip having one side of 8 cm along the strip's width. How long is this strip?
questions.a: (a) Two 8 cm × 5 cm, two 8 cm × 3 cm and two 5 cm × 3 cm. (b) The strip is made of the faces 8 × 5, 8 × 3, 8 × 5, 8 × 3 placed side by side, so its length is 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm (and its width 8 cm).

questions.q:
Prisms and pyramids are named by the polygon that forms their base (for a prism, the two congruent end faces).
(a) Find the faces, edges and vertices of a prism and of a pyramid whose base has 10 sides.
(b) A prism and a pyramid each have 36 edges. What polygon is the base of each?
(c) Show that every prism has an even number of vertices, but a pyramid can have an odd or an even number.
(d) Among prisms and pyramids, which kind can have as many faces as vertices? Show that the other kind never can.
(e) Find a prism and a pyramid that have the same number of faces as each other.
questions.a: (a) Prism: 12 faces, 30 edges, 20 vertices. Pyramid: 11 faces, 20 edges, 11 vertices. (b) Prism: 3n = 36, n = 12, a 12-sided polygon. Pyramid: 2n = 36, n = 18, an 18-sided polygon. (c) A prism has 2n vertices, always even. A pyramid has n + 1: odd when n is even (square pyramid, 5) and even when n is odd (triangular pyramid, 4). (d) Pyramids: n + 1 faces and n + 1 vertices, always equal. A prism would need n + 2 = 2n, so n = 2, and no polygon has 2 sides. (e) For example a pentagonal prism (5 + 2 = 7 faces) and a hexagonal pyramid (6 + 1 = 7 faces).
s: Part (c): 2n always even; n + 1 depends on n
Part (d): pyramids always; a prism needs n = 2, impossible
Part (e): a valid pair such as pentagonal prism and hexagonal pyramid

questions.q: A camping tent is shaped like a hexagonal pyramid: a hexagonal floor and six triangular walls that meet at the top. At every corner of the tent the tailor sews one reinforcing patch for each face (floor included) that meets at that corner. How many patches does she sew in all?

Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: A prism and a pyramid with the same n-sided base always have the same number of edges.
Statement 2: A hexagonal pyramid and a pentagonal prism have the same number of faces.
Statement 3: Every pyramid has as many faces as vertices.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q: A puzzle book asks for 'a prism with 25 edges' and 'a pyramid with 15 edges'. Show that neither solid can exist, and find the prism that has the number of edges nearest above 25.
questions.a: A prism on an n-sided base has 3n edges (n on each end face and n joining them), so its edge count is a multiple of 3; 25 is not. A pyramid on an n-sided base has 2n edges (n on the base and n to the apex), so its edge count is even; 15 is odd. The next multiple of 3 above 25 is 27, so a 9-sided (nonagonal) prism has 27 edges.
s: Prism edges are 3n, and 25 is not a multiple of 3
Pyramid edges are 2n, and 15 is odd
Nearest above: a 9-sided prism with 27 edges

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The octahedron, made by joining two square pyramids at their square bases, has 8 faces, 12 edges and 6 vertices.
Reason (R): Joining two square pyramids base to base simply doubles each of the face, edge and vertex counts of one square pyramid.
questions.a: A is true but R is false
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
A box is 10 cm long, 6 cm deep and 8 cm high. An ant is on the top face, 3 cm from the right edge and 5 cm behind the front edge. A laddu is on the right face, 2 cm behind the front edge and 2 cm below the top edge. Lina draws a net with the top face attached above the front face and the right face attached to the right of the front face, and joins the ant and the laddu with a ruler. Her line (about 8.6 cm) runs over empty paper between the top and right faces.
(a) Why is her line not a path the ant can take?
(b) Which two faces should be laid side by side instead, and how long is the straight path then?
questions.a: (a) The empty paper is not part of the box's surface, so a line passing over it does not match any path on the box. (b) The top face and the right face, unfolded about the edge they share. The ant is 3 cm from that edge and the laddu 2 cm below it, so one leg is 3 + 2 = 5 cm; the other leg is the difference in how far back they are, 5 − 2 = 3 cm. Path² = 5² + 3² = 34, so the path is √34, about 5.8 cm.
s: Part (a): the line leaves the net, so it is not on the box's surface
Part (b): top and right faces side by side, legs 5 and 3, about 5.8 cm

questions.q: True or False: To find the shortest path between two points on a cuboid, it is enough to draw any one net and join the points by a straight line, as long as the line stays inside that net. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Different ways of unfolding the cuboid can give straight lines of different lengths between the same two points, so every possible unfolding must be tried and the shortest line chosen. For example, on a 12 cm × 4 cm × 5 cm box, corner-to-opposite-corner lines on three unfoldings have squares 225, 281 and 305, so only one of them is the shortest.
s: Explains that different unfoldings give different lengths, so all must be compared

questions.q: The net of a closed cylinder is a rectangle 88 cm by 15 cm (the cylinder is 15 cm tall) with one circle touching the middle of each 88 cm side, outside the rectangle. Taking circumference = 2 × 22/7 × radius, the narrowest strip of card that holds this net, measured across the 88 cm sides, is ___ cm wide. (Write the number in digits.)

A tin of tomato puree is a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Its paper label covers the curved surface exactly. (Circumference of a circle = 2 × 22/7 × radius.)
(a) What are the length and width of the label when it is unrolled?
(b) A printer sends labels 50 cm long and 10 cm wide. How much of each label overlaps when it is wrapped once round the tin?
questions.a: (a) The label is the rectangle in the cylinder's net: length = circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm, width = height = 10 cm. (b) 50 − 44 = 6 cm overlaps.

questions.q: An ant is at the centre of the bottom face of a closed cube of edge 10 cm, and a laddu is at the centre of the top face. The ant can only walk on the outer surface. How long is its shortest path?
questions.a: 20 cm

questions.q:
A wire must be glued along the outside of a cardboard box 20 cm long, 4 cm wide and 12 cm high, using the shortest route over the surface. One end of the wire is on the front end face, midway across it and 1 cm below the top edge. The other end is on the back end face, midway across it and 1 cm above the bottom edge.
(a) Route 1 goes up the front end face, straight along the top face and down the back end face. Find its length.
(b) Route 2 crosses the front end face, a side face and the back end face. On the unfolded strip of these three faces, how far apart are the two ends, along the strip and across it?
(c) Find the length of Route 2.
(d) How much wire should be bought, and which route should be used? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 1 + 20 + 11 = 32 cm (on the unfolded strip the two ends are level, so the straight path has this length). (b) Along the strip: 2 cm (to the edge of the front end) + 20 cm + 2 cm = 24 cm. Across: the ends are at heights 11 cm and 1 cm, so 10 cm apart. (c) 24² + 10² = 576 + 100 = 676, so Route 2 is 26 cm. (d) Route 2 with 26 cm of wire, because 26 cm is shorter than 32 cm; the obvious route over the top is not the shortest.
s: Part (b): 24 cm along and 10 cm across
Part (d): Route 2, 26 cm, as it is shorter

questions.q:
An ant is at a bottom corner of a box 15 cm long, 5 cm wide and 3 cm high. A laddu is at the opposite top corner.
(a) How long is the path that runs along three edges?
(b) Find the square of the straight path length for each of the three ways of unfolding two faces.
(c) Find the shortest path.
(d) In (b), which two edges were added together in the smallest square? Make a rule for which two edges to add, and test it on a box 10 cm × 6 cm × 4 cm by finding its three squares.
(e) Another path goes along the diagonal of the 15 cm × 5 cm bottom face (√250 is about 15.81 cm) and then up a 3 cm edge. Is it shorter than your answer to (c)?
questions.a: (a) 15 + 5 + 3 = 23 cm. (b) (5 + 3)² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289; (15 + 3)² + 5² = 324 + 25 = 349; (15 + 5)² + 3² = 400 + 9 = 409. (c) 289 = 17², so the shortest path is 17 cm. (d) The smallest square, 289, adds the two shorter edges (5 + 3) and pairs them with the longest (15). Rule: add the two shorter edges. Test: (6 + 4)² + 10² = 200, (10 + 4)² + 6² = 232, (10 + 6)² + 4² = 272; the smallest again adds the two shorter edges. (e) No: 15.81 + 3 = 18.81 cm, longer than 17 cm.
s: Part (d): rule 'add the two shorter edges', tested with 200, 232 and 272

questions.q:
In a solution, d² = 5² + 12² and d = 13 cm gives the shortest path of an ant on a box, after two faces are unfolded into one plane.
(a) Describe a box and the positions of the ant and the laddu that this calculation could describe.
(b) For your box, find the length of the path that goes straight up to the edge, then along the edge, then straight back across the top face to the laddu. Is it longer or shorter than 13 cm?
(c) Explain which of the two numbers 5 and 12 had to be a sum of two distances in your situation.
questions.a: (a) For example: a box 20 cm × 20 cm × 20 cm; the ant is on the front face 8 cm below the top edge; the laddu is on the top face 4 cm behind that edge and 5 cm to the right of the ant. Unfolded, the legs are 8 + 4 = 12 and 5, giving 13 cm. (b) Going straight up 8 cm to the edge, 5 cm along the edge, then 4 cm back: 17 cm, which is longer than 13 cm. (c) In this situation 12 is the sum of the ant's distance below the edge and the laddu's distance behind it; 5 is the sideways distance along the edge.
s: Part (a): a box and positions giving legs 12 and 5 on the net
Part (b): a bent path for the box, correctly found to be longer than 13 cm
Part (c): identifies which leg is a sum of two distances

questions.q: A craft teacher wants a closed paper cone with slant length 10 cm and base radius 5 cm. Which pair of pieces is its net?
questions.a: A semicircle of radius 10 cm and a circle of radius 5 cm
o: A semicircle of radius 10 cm and a circle of radius 5 cm
A full circle of radius 10 cm and a circle of radius 5 cm
A semicircle of radius 5 cm and a circle of radius 10 cm
A quarter circle of radius 10 cm and a circle of radius 5 cm

questions.q:
A pickle factory in Guntur sells jars that are cylinders of radius 3.5 cm. Each paper label is 8 cm high and wraps once round the jar with an extra 1 cm for glue. Labels are cut from sheets 70 cm long and 25 cm wide, with the labels all lying the same way on a sheet. (Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × radius.)
(a) How long is each label?
(b) How many labels fit on a sheet if the label's length runs along the 70 cm side?
(c) How many fit if the label's length runs along the 25 cm side?
(d) The factory needs 450 labels. Which way should the labels be cut, and how many sheets will it save? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Circumference 2 × 22/7 × 3.5 = 22 cm, plus 1 cm, so 23 cm. (b) 3 labels along 70 cm (69 cm) and 3 rows in 25 cm (24 cm): 9 labels. (c) 1 label across 25 cm and 8 rows in 70 cm (64 cm): 8 labels. (d) Along the 70 cm side: 450 ÷ 9 = 50 sheets, against 450 ÷ 8 = 56.25, so 57 sheets the other way. It saves 7 sheets.
s: Part (d): along the 70 cm side, 50 sheets against 57, saving 7

questions.q: An ant is at a bottom corner of a cube of edge 6 cm and a laddu is at the opposite top corner. The ant must stay on the surface. What is the square of the length of its shortest path?
questions.a: 180 sq cm

questions.q:
An ant is on the front face of a box 40 cm long, 20 cm deep and 15 cm high, 9 cm below the top edge. A laddu is on the top face, 3 cm behind that edge and 16 cm to the right of the ant (measured along the edge).
(a) Find the length of the straight path on the net when the top face is unfolded up into the plane of the front face.
(b) Another path goes straight to the point of the edge that is directly in front of the laddu, and then straight back across the top face to the laddu. Using 16² + 9² = 337, and the fact that 18² < 337 < 19², find a range for its length.
(c) Which path should the ant take, and by at least how much is it shorter?
questions.a: (a) The legs are 9 + 3 = 12 cm and 16 cm: 12² + 16² = 144 + 256 = 400, so 20 cm. (b) The first part is between 18 cm and 19 cm, and the second part is 3 cm, so the whole path is between 21 cm and 22 cm. (c) The straight path on the net, 20 cm: it is at least 1 cm shorter than the other path, because the other path bends at the edge instead of crossing it in one straight line on the net.
s: Part (c): the 20 cm path, at least 1 cm shorter

questions.q:
Ishaan has a sheet of card 44 cm by 22 cm to make the curved part of a tin, with no overlap. He says: 'I can roll the sheet either way, and whichever way I roll it, the same two circles of radius 7 cm will close the ends.' (Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × radius.)
(a) Find the radius and height of the tin when the 44 cm side goes round.
(b) Find the radius and height when the 22 cm side goes round.
(c) Is Ishaan right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Circumference 44 cm, so radius = 44 ÷ (2 × 22/7) = 7 cm; height 22 cm. (b) Circumference 22 cm, so radius = 22 ÷ (2 × 22/7) = 3.5 cm; height 44 cm. (c) No. Both rollings make a tin, but only the first is closed by circles of radius 7 cm; the second needs circles of radius 3.5 cm, because the side that goes round must equal the circumference of the circles.
s: Part (c): verdict No, the circles must match the side that goes round

questions.q:
An octahedron's net is made of 8 equilateral triangles of side 5 cm, held together by 7 folds.
(a) How many edges does the octahedron have? (It is made by joining two square pyramids at their square bases.)
(b) Every edge that is not a fold is cut open and appears twice on the outline of the net. Find the perimeter of the net.
questions.a: (a) Each square pyramid has 4 slanting edges, and the two share the 4 base edges: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 edges. (b) 12 − 7 = 5 edges are cut, each appearing twice: 10 sides of 5 cm on the outline, so the perimeter is 50 cm.

questions.q:
The chapter says a dodecahedron, whose faces are all pentagons, has 43,380 different nets.
(a) Rohan concludes: 'With so many nets, any arrangement of its 12 pentagons joined edge to edge will fold up into a dodecahedron.' Is he right?
(b) Support your answer with what happens for a cube.
questions.a: (a) No. A large number of nets does not mean every arrangement is a net; an arrangement folds only if its faces close up without gaps or overlaps. (b) A cube has 6 square faces, yet a 2 by 3 block of six squares does not fold into a cube, and only 11 arrangements are nets.
s: Part (a): No, not every arrangement is a net
Part (b): cube example such as the 2 by 3 block that does not fold

questions.q: Paper caps shaped like cones are made from semicircles of radius 14 cm, the two halves of the straight edge being joined. (Circumference of a circle = 2 × 22/7 × radius.) What is the radius of the base of each cap?
questions.a: 7 cm

questions.q:
Two unfoldings of a box are tried for an ant's path. On the first, the straight path is the longest side of a right triangle with shorter sides 24 cm and 10 cm. On the second, the right triangle has shorter sides 20 cm and 16 cm.
(a) Find the square of the path length on each unfolding.
(b) Which unfolding gives the shorter path? Explain how you can tell without finding any square root.
questions.a: (a) First: 24² + 10² = 576 + 100 = 676 (path 26 cm). Second: 20² + 16² = 400 + 256 = 656. (b) The second. 656 is less than 676, and a smaller square means a shorter length, so the second path is shorter than 26 cm.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: No flat piece of paper can be cut to wrap a ball exactly, without wrinkles, gaps or overlaps.
Statement 2: An octahedron has the same number of different nets as a cube.
Statement 3: In the net of a cone, the curved part is a full circle whose radius equals the slant length.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q: An ant is at a bottom corner of a closed cubical sweet box of edge 8 cm. A laddu sits at the centre of the top face. How long is the ant's shortest path over the surface?
questions.a: about 12.6 cm

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When the front face and the top face of a cuboid are laid flat in one plane, the straight segment joining a point on one to a point on the other gives the shortest path between them over those two faces.
Reason (R): When two faces that share an edge are laid flat about that edge, every path across that edge keeps its length, so a straight segment on the flat picture of those two faces is a path of the same length on the box.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
