questions.q:
For a school band, Meera makes a drum and a cap from chart paper. (Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × radius.)
The drum is a closed cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 20 cm. The cap is a cone made from a quarter circle of radius 28 cm, the two straight edges being joined.
(a) Give the shapes and measurements of the pieces in the drum's net.
(b) What is the slant length of the cap?
(c) Find the circumference and the radius of the cap's base.
(d) Her friend uses a semicircle of radius 28 cm instead. Find the radius of the base of his cap.
(e) Whose cap fits exactly on the top rim of the drum? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Two circles of radius 7 cm and a rectangle 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm long and 20 cm wide. (b) The radius of the quarter circle, 28 cm. (c) The curved edge of the quarter circle becomes the base rim: (1/4) × 2 × 22/7 × 28 = 44 cm, so the base radius is 7 cm. (d) Half of 2 × 22/7 × 28 = 88 cm, so the base radius is 14 cm. (e) Meera's: its base rim is 44 cm, the same as the drum's rim (radius 7 cm); her friend's base is 88 cm round, twice the drum's.
s: Part (a): two circles of radius 7 cm and a 44 cm × 20 cm rectangle
Part (c): base circumference 44 cm, radius 7 cm
Part (e): Meera's cap, rims both 44 cm

questions.q: In a dark room a torch shines on a rectangular cut-out 30 cm by 20 cm, with the beam perpendicular to the wall behind it. The 30 cm edges are parallel to the wall, but the cut-out is tilted so that one 30 cm edge is 16 cm closer to the wall than the other. The torch is moved very far back. The shadow becomes almost exactly a rectangle of what size?
questions.a: 30 cm by 12 cm

questions.q: An engineering drawing gives only two views of a solid: its front view is a triangle and the outline of its top view is a square. Which could the solid be?
questions.a: A square pyramid or a triangular prism
o: A square pyramid or a triangular prism
A cone or a square pyramid

questions.q: Eight identical cubes stand in four stacks on a 2-by-2 grid. In the back row the stacks are 3 cubes (left) and 1 cube (right); in the front row they are 2 cubes (left) and 2 cubes (right). The greatest number of cubes that can be taken off the tops of stacks without changing the front view, the top view or the side view (seen from the right) is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

A school fixes a flat solar panel 2.6 m long (measured along its slope) on a roof ledge. The panel's lower edge rests on the ledge and its upper edge is raised. The ledge offers only 2.45 m of horizontal space, measured straight under the panel. The panel works best when it is as close to flat as possible, but it must fit the ledge.
(a) If the upper edge is 1 m higher than the lower edge, how much horizontal space (the panel's top view) does it take?
(b) If the upper edge is only 0.6 m higher, the square of the horizontal space is 2.6² − 0.6² = 6.4. Does the panel fit? (Use 2.5² = 6.25.)
(c) If the upper edge is 2.4 m higher, how much horizontal space does it take?
(d) Of these three heights, which should the school choose? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 2.6² − 1² = 6.76 − 1 = 5.76 = 2.4², so 2.4 m. (b) 6.4 is more than 6.25, so the space needed is more than 2.5 m, which is more than 2.45 m: it does not fit. (c) 2.6² − 2.4² = 6.76 − 5.76 = 1, so 1 m. (d) The 1 m rise: it fits (2.4 m ≤ 2.45 m) and is flatter than the 2.4 m rise; the 0.6 m rise is flatter but does not fit.
s: Part (b): more than 2.5 m, does not fit
Part (d): the 1 m rise, the flattest one that fits

questions.q:
A square card lies flat on the floor. It is then tilted about one of its diagonals, which stays on the floor.
(a) What shape is the projection of the card on the floor? Give a reason.
(b) Describe a position of the card in which its projection on the floor is a line segment.
questions.a: (a) A rhombus (not a square). The diagonal on the floor keeps its length; the other diagonal is tilted, so its projection is shorter. The diagonals still bisect each other at right angles, so the four sides are equal but the diagonals are unequal. (b) When the card stands upright, perpendicular to the floor, its projection is a line segment.
s: Part (a): rhombus, one diagonal kept and the other shortened
Part (b): card perpendicular to the floor gives a segment

questions.q:
A rod AB is held above a table. End A is 9 cm above the table and end B is 21 cm above it. Its projection on the table is 16 cm long.
(a) Find the length of the rod.
(b) End B is now lowered until both ends are 9 cm above the table. What is the length of the projection now, and why?
questions.a: (a) Draw from A a line parallel to the table, meeting the vertical through B at E. AE = projection = 16 cm and BE = 21 − 9 = 12 cm, with a right angle at E. AB² = 16² + 12² = 400, so AB = 20 cm. (b) 20 cm: the rod is now parallel to the table, and only then does the projection equal the actual length.
s: Part (b): 20 cm because the rod is parallel to the table

questions.q:
Four identical cubes are glued in an L: three in a row from left to right on the table, and the fourth on top of the left cube.
(a) Describe the front view and the side view seen from the right.
(b) One more cube is to be glued on so that the front view does not change but the top view does. Give one place where it can go, and explain.
questions.a: (a) Front view: an L of 4 squares, a row of 3 with one more square above the left one. Side view: 2 squares, one above the other, since from the right all the cubes line up behind each other and the stack is 2 high. (b) Directly behind or directly in front of any one of the four cubes (for example behind the right-hand cube, on the table). From the front it lines up with a cube already there, so the front view is unchanged; from above it covers a new square behind or in front of the row, so the top view changes.
s: Part (a): front view an L of 4 squares, side view a column of 2
Part (b): directly behind or in front of a cube: front view unchanged, new square in the top view

questions.q: True or False: Two rods of equal length are held parallel to each other above the floor, not upright, and the plane containing them is not upright either. In sunlight falling perpendicular to the floor, their shadows are also parallel and of equal length. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. Joining the ends of the two rods gives a parallelogram (one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel). The projection of a parallelogram is always a parallelogram, and its opposite sides are equal and parallel; those opposite sides are the two shadows. (The shadows may be shorter than the rods, but they are shortened equally.)
s: Uses the parallelogram formed by the rods and its projection being a parallelogram

questions.q: A rectangular card is held in sunlight that falls perpendicular to the floor, and it is turned to many different positions. Which of these can NOT be the shape of its shadow on the floor?
questions.a: A trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides
o: A trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides
A parallelogram with no right angle
A rectangle narrower than the card

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about projections onto a plane.
Statement 1: The projection of a line segment is never longer than the segment itself.
Statement 2: The projection of a line segment can be a single point.
Statement 3: A square and a rectangle that is not a square can have the same projection.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A student's notebook records two observations of shadows cast by sunlight falling perpendicular to the floor:
(i) 'The shadow of a parallelogram-shaped card was a trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides.'
(ii) 'The shadow of a 10 cm stick was 12 cm long.'
Show that both observations are impossible.
questions.a: (i) Such a shadow is the card's projection on the floor. Projection keeps parallel lines parallel, so both pairs of opposite sides of the parallelogram stay parallel in the shadow. The shadow is always a parallelogram, never a trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides. (ii) The stick, its shadow and the vertical difference in height of its ends form a right triangle with the stick as the longest side, so the shadow is at most 10 cm (equal only when the stick is parallel to the floor). 12 cm is impossible.
s: (i): so the shadow is a parallelogram, not such a trapezium
(ii): the projection is at most the actual length, so 12 cm is impossible

questions.q:
Eleven identical cubes stand on a 3-by-3 grid. Stacks, left to right: back row 2, 3, 1; middle row 1, 0, 2; front row 1, 1, 0.
(a) Give the heights of the columns in the front view.
(b) Give the heights of the rows in the side view (back, middle, front).
(c) How many squares make up the top view?
(d) Name one stack that cannot be seen at all in the front view, and say why it is hidden.
(e) What is the fewest number of cubes that must be added so that the front view becomes three columns of height 3 while the top view stays the same?
questions.a: (a) 2, 3, 2 (the tallest stack in each column). (b) 3, 2, 1. (c) 7 squares (the two empty places are the middle of the middle row and the right of the front row). (d) The middle-left stack (1 cube) is hidden behind the front-left stack, which is just as tall; likewise the back-right stack (1 cube) is hidden behind the middle-right stack of 2. (e) Column 1 needs a stack of 3: raise the back-left stack from 2 to 3 (1 cube). Column 3 needs a 3: raise the middle-right stack from 2 to 3 (1 cube). Column 2 already has 3. So 2 cubes.
s: Part (d): a stack hidden behind one at least as tall in the same column

questions.q:
A solid has a front view that is a rectangle 6 cm wide and 4 cm high, and a top view that is a rectangle 6 cm wide and 3 cm deep.
(a) Describe two different solids that both have these two views.
(b) Give the side view of each of your solids.
(c) Explain why engineers draw all three views.
questions.a: (a) For example: a cuboid 6 cm × 3 cm × 4 cm; and a triangular prism 6 cm long lying on its 6 cm × 3 cm rectangular face, whose triangular ends have a 3 cm base and a 4 cm vertical side at the back, so the ends are right triangles. (b) Cuboid: a rectangle 3 cm wide and 4 cm high. Prism: a right triangle with a 3 cm base and a 4 cm height. (c) Two views can come from different objects; the third view helps tell them apart (even three views do not always fix an object).
s: Part (a): two different solids with both views
Part (b): correct side view for each
Part (c): a projection does not decide the object, so more views are needed

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm, standing on one circular face, has a square as its front view.
Reason (R): If an object passes perpendicularly through a plane, the hole it makes has the same shape as its projection on that plane.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
A museum orders an exhibit built from identical wooden cubes costing Rs 40 each, standing on a 3-by-3 grid. The designer sends only three views. Top view: 7 squares are covered; the back-left and front-right squares are empty. Front view: columns of heights 1, 3, 2 (left to right). Side view: rows of heights 3, 2, 1 (back, middle, front).
(a) Which square must hold a stack of 3? Explain.
(b) Find the greatest number of cubes the exhibit can have.
(c) Find the least number of cubes, and give that arrangement.
(d) The museum has Rs 420 and wants the exhibit to match all three views. Can it be built, and with how many cubes? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The back-middle square. The 3 must be in the middle column (front view) and in the back row (side view); the back row's middle square is the only square in both. (b) Each stack as tall as its column and row allow: back row 0, 3, 2; middle row 1, 2, 2; front row 1, 1, 0: 12 cubes. (c) Back row 0, 3, 1; middle row 1, 1, 2; front row 1, 1, 0: 10 cubes. (Every covered square needs 1 cube; the back-middle needs 3; column 3 and the middle row each need a 2, which the middle-right stack gives.) (d) Yes, with 10 cubes: Rs 400. Rs 420 buys only 10 cubes, and 10 is exactly the least number that matches the views, so the museum must use the arrangement in (c).
s: Part (a): back-middle square, the only one in both the middle column and the back row
Part (c): 10 cubes with a valid arrangement
Part (d): yes, 10 cubes for Rs 400, the least arrangement

questions.q:
A cube of edge 10 cm stands on a table, turned so that one vertical edge points straight at you and two side faces slope away equally.
(a) What shape is the front view, and what are its height and width?
(b) Is the width more or less than 14 cm? Show how you know without a calculator.
questions.a: (a) A rectangle 10 cm high; its width is the diagonal of the square top face, as seen from the front. (b) The diagonal squared is 10² + 10² = 200, and 14² = 196 is less than 200, so the width is more than 14 cm.
s: Part (a): rectangle of height 10 cm, width equal to the face diagonal

questions.q: In a cartoon, a solid bursts straight through a paper wall, moving perpendicular to it, and leaves a perfectly circular hole. Which solid could NOT have made this hole, however it was turned?
questions.a: A cube

questions.q:
Match each solid with its front view, top view and side view (seen from the right), in that order.
Column A:
1. Cylinder lying on its curved surface, its length running from front to back
2. Square pyramid standing on its base
3. Triangular prism lying on a rectangular face, its triangular ends facing left and right
4. Cone standing on its base
Column B:
(P) triangle, square with both diagonals, triangle
(Q) triangle, circle with its centre marked, triangle
(R) circle, rectangle, rectangle
(S) rectangle, rectangle with a line along its middle, triangle

Identical cubes stand on a grid of 2 rows and 3 columns, and the top view shows all 6 squares. The front view has columns of heights 3, 1 and 2 (left to right), and the side view has rows of heights 3 (back) and 2 (front).
(a) Find the greatest number of cubes the arrangement can have.
(b) Find the least number of cubes, and give that arrangement.
(c) Explain why the three views do not fix the number of cubes.
questions.a: (a) Each stack can be as tall as both its column and its row allow: back row 3, 1, 2 and front row 2, 1, 2, so 11 cubes. (b) Every square needs at least 1 cube; the 3 must be in the back-left stack (the only place where column 1 and the back row both allow 3), and a 2 must appear in column 3 and in the front row, which one stack (front-right) can do. Back row 3, 1, 1; front row 1, 1, 2: 9 cubes. (c) Hidden stacks behind or beside taller ones can be changed without changing what is seen from the front, top or side, so different arrangements (9, 10 or 11 cubes) give the same views.
s: Part (b): 9 cubes with a valid arrangement
Part (c): stacks hidden by taller ones can change without changing the views

questions.q: At noon the sun's rays fall perpendicular to a table. A 26 cm stick held slanting above the table casts a shadow 24 cm long on it. Jaya says one end of the stick is 26 − 24 = 2 cm higher than the other. How much higher is it really?
questions.a: 10 cm

questions.q:
A thin rod has one end on the floor in the corner of a room. Its other end is 8 cm above the floor, and the point of the floor directly below it is 12 cm from one wall and 9 cm from the other.
(a) Find the length of its top view (projection on the floor).
(b) Find the length of the rod.
(c) The front view and side view have lengths whose squares are 12² + 8² and 9² + 8². Are all three views shorter than the rod? Explain why, using the chapter's idea.
(d) The rod is now laid flat on the floor, pointing 15 cm to the right and 8 cm back. Which view now has the rod's full length, and how long are the other two views?
(e) Check that in both positions the squares of the three view lengths add up to twice the square of the rod's length.
questions.a: (a) 12² + 9² = 144 + 81 = 225, so 15 cm. (b) The top view (15 cm) and the height (8 cm) are at right angles: 15² + 8² = 289, so 17 cm. (c) Yes: 208 and 145 are less than 289, and 225 < 289. A projection equals the actual length only when the rod is parallel to that plane, and this rod is parallel to none of the three. (d) The top view is 17 cm (parallel to the floor). The front view is 15 cm and the side view is 8 cm. (e) First position: 208 + 225 + 145 = 578 = 2 × 289. Second: 225 + 289 + 64 = 578 = 2 × 289.
s: Part (c): all shorter, since the rod is parallel to none of the planes
Part (d): top view 17 cm, front 15 cm, side 8 cm

questions.q:
Arun says: 'The top view of a stack of identical cubes shows the length and width it covers, and the front view shows the height of each column. So the three views always tell exactly how many cubes are in the stack.'
(a) Test his second sentence on this case: a grid of 2 rows and 3 columns, all 6 squares in the top view, front view columns of heights 3, 2, 2 (left to right), side view rows of heights 3 (back) and 1 (front).
(b) Test it again on a 2-by-2 grid with all 4 squares in the top view, front view columns of heights 3 and 3, and side view rows of heights 3 and 3. Give the least and greatest numbers of cubes.
(c) Give your verdict on Arun's statement as a whole.
questions.a: (a) The front row is only 1 high, so each front stack is 1 cube. The back row must then give each column its height: 3, 2, 2. Only one arrangement fits, with 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 10 cubes, so here the views do fix the number. (b) Each column and each row needs a stack of 3. Two stacks of 3 on a diagonal and 1 cube on each other square give the least, 8 cubes; four stacks of 3 give the greatest, 12 cubes. The number is not fixed. (c) Partly right: the first sentence is correct, and sometimes the views fix the count, as in (a), but not always, as (b) shows, because a projection does not decide the object. (A reasoned 'No', that the views do not always fix the count, also earns the mark.)
s: Part (b): least 8, greatest 12, so not fixed
Part (c): verdict partly right or No, with the reason that the views fix the count in some cases but not always

questions.q:
A student draws on isometric paper, edge by edge: up 2 units along the height axis, 1 unit along the length axis, down 1 unit, 1 unit along the length axis, down 1 unit, and then 2 units opposite to the length axis.
(a) Does the drawing return to its starting point? Show how you know.
(b) What does the closed outline show, and how many unit squares does it enclose on the real solid?
questions.a: (a) Yes. Height: +2 − 1 − 1 = 0. Length: +1 + 1 − 2 = 0. (b) The face of a two-step staircase, with steps 2 and 1 units high; it encloses 2 + 1 = 3 unit squares.
s: Part (a): height and length moves both total 0
Part (b): a two-step staircase face of 3 unit squares

questions.q:
A drawing instruction says: 'From a corner, go 2 units along the length axis, 3 units up the height axis, 2 units opposite to the length axis, then 3 units down.'
(a) What shape does this trace on the real solid?
(b) What does the traced shape look like on the isometric paper, and what are its angles?
(c) Write a similar instruction that traces the top face of a cuboid 2 units long and 3 units deep.
questions.a: (a) A rectangle 2 units by 3 units on a vertical face of the solid. (b) A parallelogram with sides 2 and 3 units, because a vertical grid line meets a slanting grid line at 60° and 120°; its angles are 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°. (c) For example: 'From a top corner, go 2 units along the length axis, 3 units along the depth axis, 2 units opposite to the length axis, then 3 units opposite to the depth axis.'
s: Part (a): a 2 by 3 rectangle on a vertical face
Part (b): a parallelogram with angles 60° and 120°
Part (c): a correct closed instruction using length and depth

questions.q:
An isometric drawing shows a solid staircase of unit cubes. Its front face shows three steps, 1, 2 and 3 cubes high from left to right, and every edge along the depth direction is drawn 2 units long. Meena says: 'The front face shows 1 + 2 + 3 squares, so the staircase is made of exactly 6 cubes.'
(a) What does the 2-unit depth edge tell you about the staircase?
(b) How many cubes does the solid staircase contain?
(c) Is Meena right?
questions.a: (a) Lengths along the depth axis are drawn true to the unit, so the staircase is 2 cubes deep: the front layer has a second identical layer behind it. (b) 2 × (1 + 2 + 3) = 12 cubes. (c) No. She counted only the front layer and ignored the depth axis.
s: Part (a): the staircase is 2 units deep
Part (c): verdict No, the depth was ignored

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about isometric drawing.
Statement 1: On isometric paper, the height axis may be drawn along either of the two slanting grid directions.
Statement 2: Every length in an isometric drawing of a cube, including the diagonals of its faces, is in the same proportion to the real length.
Statement 3: A glass cube drawn in isometric projection shows 12 edges, all of equal length on the paper.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only

questions.q: The chapter shows 5 flat Tetris shapes made by gluing four cubes face to face. How many more ways of gluing four cubes give a shape that does not lie flat, if a shape and its mirror image count as different when one cannot be turned to match the other (so a left-handed and a right-handed twist count as two shapes)?

For a school display, solid blocks are built as n × n × n cubes from unit cubes and shown in an isometric view, so that only the top face, the front face and the right face can be seen. A cube is 'visible' if at least one of its faces can be seen. Only visible cubes will be painted.
(a) How many cubes are visible for n = 2 and for n = 3?
(b) The hidden cubes always form one block. Describe it for an n × n × n cube.
(c) Use (b) to predict the number of visible cubes for n = 4.
(d) There is paint for 40 cubes. What is the largest block that can be displayed with all its visible cubes painted? Justify.
questions.a: (a) n = 2: 8 − 1 = 7. n = 3: 27 − 8 = 19. (b) The cubes not on the top, front or right layer form an (n − 1) × (n − 1) × (n − 1) cube at the back, left and bottom. (c) 64 − 27 = 37. (d) n = 4: 37 visible cubes fit the paint for 40; n = 5 would need 125 − 64 = 61.

questions.q:
(a) In the isometric drawing of a unit cube, the top face is a rhombus made of two equilateral triangles of the grid. How long is its shorter diagonal on the paper?
(b) On the real cube, the diagonal of a face is the longest side of a right triangle whose other sides are edges. Is the shorter diagonal in the drawing shown in true proportion to the edges? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 1 unit, the same as an edge, because it is a side of an equilateral triangle of the grid. (b) No. The real face diagonal is longer than an edge, but the drawing shows it equal to an edge (and the other diagonal even longer than it). Only lengths along the three axes are kept in proportion.
s: Part (b): not in proportion; only lengths along the three axes are

questions.q:
A cube made of glass is balanced on a corner and drawn as its isometric projection.
(a) How many edges are drawn, and how do their lengths compare?
(b) The corner at the bottom and the corner at the top both project to the same point. Where on the hexagon is that point?
(c) Explain why the finished drawing looks like a regular hexagon with all three of its long diagonals drawn.
questions.a: (a) All 12 edges are drawn, all of equal length. (b) At the centre of the hexagon. (c) The 6 edges not touching the top or bottom corner form the hexagon's outline. The 3 edges from the top corner and the 3 from the bottom corner all run from the centre to the six vertices of the hexagon, one to each, so together they make the three long diagonals.
s: Part (b): the centre of the hexagon
Part (c): 6 outline edges plus 6 half-diagonals from the centre

questions.q:
A solid is a slab 2 units long, 2 units deep and 1 unit high, with one more unit cube on top at the back-left corner (farthest along the depth axis and nearest the start of the length axis). It is drawn on isometric paper in the usual view, showing the faces that point up, to the front and to the right; in this view no part of any face is hidden by another cube.
(a) How many unit squares are seen facing up, facing the front and facing the right?
(b) Asha says: 'The drawing shows 10 unit squares, so the solid is made of 10 unit cubes.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Up: the slab's 4 top squares, less the 1 covered by the cube, plus the cube's top: 4. Front: 2 on the slab and 1 on the cube, which stands above the back row so its front face shows: 3. Right: 2 on the slab and 1 on the cube: 3. (b) No. There are 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 squares but only 4 + 1 = 5 cubes: the squares count faces, and most cubes show more than one face (the cube on top shows three, the front-right slab cube shows three, and the back-left slab cube shows none).
s: Part (b): No, 5 cubes; squares count faces and one cube can show several

questions.q:
The straight Tetris piece, a row of 4 unit cubes, is drawn on isometric paper as one block in three ways: along the height axis, along the length axis and along the depth axis.
(a) In which drawing are the vertical lines longest, and how long are they? How long are they in the other two?
(b) The piece is made of glass and drawn along the length axis with its hidden edges dashed. How many dashed edges are there, and what is their total length?
questions.a: (a) Along the height axis: its vertical lines are 4 units, because vertical on the paper always means height. In the other two drawings the piece is 1 unit high, so its vertical lines are 1 unit. (b) The block is 4 long, 1 deep and 1 high. The 3 edges meeting at the one corner that cannot be seen are hidden, one along each axis: 4 + 1 + 1 = 6 units of dashed line.
s: Part (a): height-axis drawing, 4 units; 1 unit in the other two

questions.q:
Each block of unit cubes is drawn on isometric paper so that its top, front and right faces are seen. Match each block with the number of unit squares that can be seen.
Column A:
1. A single unit cube
2. A slab 3 units long, 2 units deep and 1 unit high
3. A tower of 3 cubes along the height axis
4. A slab 2 units long, 2 units deep and 1 unit high
Column B:
(P) 3
(Q) 11
(R) 7
(S) 8

The isometric projection of a cube balanced on a corner is a regular hexagon. Its three visible edges meet at the centre.
(a) Explain why the hexagon splits into 6 equilateral triangles, using the fact that all projected edges are equal. (The three hidden edges also run from the centre, to the other three vertices.)
(b) Hence find each angle of the hexagon.
(c) Each face appears as a rhombus. Find its angles.
(d) A 2 × 2 × 2 cube of unit cubes is drawn the same way, showing the lines between the unit cubes. How many small rhombuses can be seen?
(e) How many small triangles of the isometric grid does its outline cover?
questions.a: (a) Each triangle has two sides that are edges from the centre and one side that is an outline edge; all are projected edges, so all three sides are equal. (b) Each angle of the hexagon is made of two 60° angles: 120°. (c) Each rhombus is two of these triangles: angles 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°. (d) 3 visible faces × 4 = 12 rhombuses. (e) 12 rhombuses × 2 triangles = 24 small triangles (a hexagon of side 2 holds 6 × 4 = 24).
s: Part (a): every triangle has three equal projected edges

questions.q:
An architect's office in Pune asks a junior to draw a box 4 units long, 2 units deep and 3 units high on isometric paper. In his drawing, each of the three visible vertical lines is 4 units, each edge along the length axis is 3 units, and each edge along the depth axis is 2 units.
(a) What box does his drawing actually show?
(b) Which two measurements has he swapped?
(c) How many unit segments make up the visible edges of his drawing, and of a correct drawing?
(d) The senior says: 'The two counts match, so the drawing can go to the carpenter.' Should it go? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A box 4 units high, 3 units long and 2 units deep. (b) The length (4) and the height (3). (c) Both have 3 × (4 + 2 + 3) = 27 unit segments. (d) No, it must be redrawn. Equal totals do not mean the same box: vertical lines on isometric paper always mean height, so the carpenter would build a box 4 high and 3 long, standing up instead of lying along its length.
s: Part (d): redraw; equal counts do not give the same box, vertical always means height

questions.q: True or False: A cube resting on one edge, with the two faces at that edge sloping equally, does not give an isometric projection on the floor. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. A projection is isometric only when all 12 projected edges are equal. Resting on an edge, the 4 edges parallel to that edge are parallel to the floor and keep their true length, while the other 8 edges are tilted, so their projections are shorter. The edges are unequal, so it is not isometric; balancing the cube on a corner is what makes all of them equal.
s: 4 edges keep their true length and 8 tilted edges are shorter, so the projected edges are not all equal

questions.q: An isometric drawing shows the top, front and right faces of a solid made of unit cubes, each of these faces being a 2 by 2 grid of unit squares. How many unit cubes could the solid be made of?
questions.a: 7 or 8

questions.q: A 3 × 3 × 3 cube built from 27 unit cubes is drawn on isometric paper so that its top, front and right faces are seen. The unit cube at the top-front-right corner is then removed and the drawing is redone. The number of unit squares that can be seen in the new drawing is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

(a) A cube rests on one face on the floor and is projected straight down. How many of its 12 edges have projections as long as the real edge, and what happens to the others?
(b) The same cube is balanced on a corner and projected down. The projections of all 12 edges are now equal to each other. Are they as long as the real edge? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The 8 horizontal edges (the top 4 and the bottom 4, which project onto the same square) keep their true length, because they are parallel to the floor. The 4 vertical edges project to single points. (b) No. Balanced on a corner, no edge is parallel to the floor, and a projection equals the true length only when the segment is parallel to the plane, so every projected edge is shorter than the real one (but all are equal).
s: Part (a): 8 edges at true length, 4 vertical edges become points
Part (b): No, no edge is parallel to the floor, so each projection is shorter

questions.q:
A cuboid 3 units long, 2 units deep and 4 units high is drawn on isometric paper.
(a) How many edges are visible, and what is the total of their lengths in grid units?
(b) How many of the visible edges run straight up the page, and what is their total length?
(c) If the hidden edges are drawn dashed, how many are there and what is their total length?
(d) Check that (a) and (c) together give the total length of all 12 edges of the cuboid.
(e) The outline of the drawing is a hexagon. Describe its pairs of opposite sides.
questions.a: (a) 9 visible edges, three along each axis: 3 × 3 + 3 × 2 + 3 × 4 = 27 units. (b) 3 vertical edges, 3 × 4 = 12 units. (c) 3 hidden edges, one along each axis: 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 units. (d) 27 + 9 = 36 = 4 × (3 + 2 + 4), the total of 4 edges of each length. (e) Opposite sides are parallel and equal: two vertical sides of 4 units, two sides of 3 units along the length axis, and two sides of 2 units along the depth axis.
s: Part (e): opposite sides parallel and equal: 4 and 4, 3 and 3, 2 and 2
